## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Udumbarajātaka* (Ja 298) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. The story opens with the verse incipit *Udumbarā c’ ime pakkā* ("Ripe are these figs") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework recorded in the text, the Buddha recounted this birth story while residing at Jetavana monastery, occasioned by a certain monk who had established a hermitage at a frontier village (*paccantagāma*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story's concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the resident small monkey (*khuddamakkato nevāsiko*) and the visiting large black monkey (*kāḷamahāmakkato āgantuko*) represented figures from the present circumstance, whereas the Bodhisatta was the tree devatā (*rukkhadevatā*) who observed and commented upon the encounter [Fausböll 1879].

Regarding textual parallels and reuse, SuttaCentral lists no external cross-canonical parallels for this discourse [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus identifies internal Pali parallels solely within the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), comprising four matching segments totaling 351 shared characters (with the longest matching sequence spanning segments §0.4–1.4 against §2933_5–2936 at 0.8 similarity), reflecting canonical verse transmission preserved inside the prose commentary [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects no cross-language parallels meeting the standard threshold [DharmaNexus]. Four modern translations are recorded in four languages on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral].
